title: Pulmonary hydatid cyst misdiagnosed as lung cancer
case_text: A 47-year-old woman, without past medical history, presented with a 3-month history of hemoptysis. The episodes were intermittent, with an estimated daily volume of less than 50 mL, and were not accompanied by other respiratory symptoms such as dyspnea, chest pain, or fever. She denied systemic symptoms, including weight loss, night sweats, or fatigue. The patient was a non-smoker and had no history of close contact with dogs or other animals. Family history was negative for malignancies, tuberculosis, or chronic respiratory conditions. The physical examination was normal, and laboratory findings were within normal ranges. Chest x-ray revealed a right lung round opacity with irregular contours (Fig. 1A). Computed tomography showed a mass with spiculated margins and central necrosis, located in the apical segment of the right lower lobe (Fig. 1B), moderately contrast- enhanced, measuring 4 x 2.8 x 3.2 cm (Fig. 1C). No abnormalities were detected in the abdomen. A scan guided biopsy was performed showing inflammatory pulmonary parenchyma with no signs of malignancy. Complete blood count did not reveal eosinophilia and hydatid serelogy was negative. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed significant bleeding from the superior segmental bronchus of right lower lobe. Furthermore, no endobronchial lesion was detected. Pathology examination of the bronchial aspiration revealed bronchial cells isolated or grouped in clusters and showing an anisokaryosis with voluminous ovoid or elongated nuclei with finely distributed non-nucleated chromatin, suggestive of malignant cells (Fig. 2A). Regarding those findings, lung carcinoma was highly suspected and the importance of hemoptysis motivated an urgent hemostasis lobectomy. On exploration, a 4 cm intraparenchymal firm mass was found. The patient then underwent a right lower lobectomy with radical lymph node dissection via a right posterolateral thoracotomy. Gross examination revealed a cystic formation measuring 4 cm long with a whitish, thin wall. The histological examination showed a hydatid cyst composed of a laminated membrane lined by a proligerous membrane made up of a layer of eosinophilic cells (Fig. 2B), confirming the diagnosis of pulmonary hydatid cyst. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on the 6th postoperative day. Recurrence was not detected during four years follow-up.
